fixes.explanation: Not quite. Daniel 11:2 says the fourth king will be far richer than all the others. Other kings come before him, and he outdoes every one of them. Money is his big thing in this verse.
Babylon sounds right, and it's a name you'd expect to hear. But the text says his wealth stirs up everyone against the kingdom of Greece. That's a whole lot of money pointed at one target, friend.

The text goes another way. The verse calls him one of the king of the South's commanders, and says he grows even stronger and rules his own kingdom with great authority. Ruling his own kingdom is the part this answer skips, friend.
The verse doesn't say anything like that. It says the commander himself grows even stronger and rules his own kingdom with great authority. His army isn't mentioned at all.
Right, to seal the agreement. After some years they form an alliance, and the daughter goes to the king of the North to seal it. That's the reason the text gives.

No peace talks in this verse. The one from her family line rises up, comes against the army of the king of the North and enters his fortress, fighting and prevailing. Fighting and prevailing is the opposite of a handshake, friend.

Right. The text says, “He will take even their gods captive to Egypt…” and the metal images and precious vessels of silver and gold come along with them. It's a whole moving truck of the North's treasures. That's quite a haul, friend.

Priests aren't named in this verse. It says he takes their gods captive to Egypt, with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold. The list is gods, images and vessels, and priests aren't on it.
Horses don't show up in the list. Verse 8 says gods, metal images, and precious vessels of silver and gold, all taken to Egypt. That's the whole list, friend.

That's right. The sons stir up strife and assemble a great army, which advances forcefully, sweeping through like a flood. A flood doesn't ask permission, friend. Strife comes first, and then the army.
Ships aren't mentioned here. Daniel 11:10 says the sons assemble a great army, and it advances forcefully like a flood. This verse is all army, friend.
That's not what the text says. In a rage, the king of the South marches out to fight. Marching out is the opposite of hiding behind walls, friend.

Right. When the army is carried off, the king of the South will be proud in heart and cast down tens of thousands, but he will not triumph. Proud heart, tens of thousands cast down, and still no triumph. Winning the fight without winning the whole thing is a strange spot to be in.

That's right. The king of the North will raise another army, larger than the first, with many supplies. He lost one army and came back with a bigger one. Daniel 11:13 says he does it after some years.
Not the same size. Verse 13 says the new army is larger than the first, and it comes with many supplies. Same size? This king isn't here to repeat himself, friend.
Rule is a big word, but it's not what the verse says. The violent ones will exalt themselves, but they will fail. The verse lands on that word, friend.
Yes. The forces of the South will not stand, and even their best troops won't be able to resist. When the best can't hold, you know it's a hard day. Verse 15 says it plainly, friend.
That's it. He gives him a daughter in marriage in order to overthrow the kingdom. The agreement and the plan are two different things. Daniel 11:17 puts them side by side.
Verse 17 doesn't mention that. What he gives is a daughter in marriage, in order to overthrow the kingdom. A share of his kingdom isn't in the text.
That's right. Daniel 11:17 says his plan will not succeed or help him. All that scheming, and the plan goes nowhere. Not succeeding is the whole story of that plan.

Yes. After he turns his face to the coastlands and captures many of them, a commander puts an end to his reproach and turns it back upon him. He gets a taste of his own medicine. The reproach he dished out comes right back around.
Right. Daniel 11:20 says within a few days he will be destroyed, though not in anger or in battle. So the battle part of the card is what doesn't fit. The text says how it won't happen, friend.

That's it. Royal honors will not be given to him, but he comes in a time of peace and seizes the kingdom by intrigue. Intrigue is how he seizes it. It's peace on the outside and scheming doing the work.
Verse 21 says royal honors will not be given to him. It says he seizes the kingdom by intrigue. The king of the South handing it over isn't in the text.
That's right. Daniel 11:23 says that after an alliance is made with him, he will act deceitfully. He rises to power with only a few people, yet he acts deceitfully. Watch who you shake hands with.
Yes. He lavishes plunder, loot, and wealth on his followers. I bet his followers have no complaints. Verse 24 names them as the ones who get it.
The text doesn't send it south. It says he lavishes plunder, loot, and wealth on his followers. Followers are who the verse names, friend.

Right. The king of the South mobilizes a very large and powerful army, but he will not withstand the plots devised against him. A big army, and still the plots get him. Plans made against him are what he can't stand up to.
No storm in this verse. His army is very large and powerful, but verse 25 says he will not withstand the plots devised against him. A storm isn't the threat here, friend. The plots are.
Yes. Those who eat from his provisions will seek to destroy him. It's like biting the hand that fills the cookie jar. The people eating his provisions are the ones seeking to destroy him.

Seeing through lies sounds smart, but that's not the reason in the text. The lies are to no avail because the end will still come at the appointed time (Daniel 11:27). They can lie across that table all day, friend, and the appointed time doesn't move.

Officials don't come into this verse. The two kings speak lies at the same table, but to no avail, for still the end will come at the appointed time. Verse 27 gives one reason, and it's the appointed time.
Right. The ships of Kittim come against him, and he will lose heart and turn back. All that power, and his heart drops when the ships show up. The ships of Kittim are what do it.

That's right. Daniel 11:30 says he will return and show favor to those who forsake the holy covenant. The favor goes to the people walking away from it. Rage first, then favor for those who forsake it.

Follow is a fair guess, but it's not the word in the verse. Verse 32 says the people who know their God will firmly resist him. The flattery corrupts those who violate the covenant, and these people hold firm.
